item.title: Vercel moved to kill static credentials. Then developers spotted its own deployment token.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:

The post Vercel moved to kill static credentials. Then developers spotted its own deployment token. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Vercel wants to eliminate long-lived API keys from its ecosystem, and it is giving Marketplace vendors until January 2027 to comply or risk being delisted, a push that lands as a run of credential-stealing supply chain attacks — including a recent npm worm that scraped tokens straight out of CI pipelines — keeps proving how much damage a single leaked secret can do.

Vercel’s own GitHub Actions deployment workflow still relies on the kind of persistent credential the company now wants gone.

Developers have already pointed out a complication, though: Vercel’s own GitHub Actions deployment workflow still relies on the kind of persistent credential the company now wants gone.

In a Thursday announcement, Vercel CTO Malte Ubl says the company surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported what Vercel considers secure authentication methods, and it is now pushing OpenID Connect (OIDC) and short-lived, identity-based tokens as the alternative to static API keys that can stay valid indefinitely.

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch amplifies the message on X, writing that it is “time to kill ‘static credentials’” and arguing that while attacks and breaches can still happen, stolen credentials should behave more like “self-destructing keys” that expire before an attacker can keep using them.

Vercel’s deployment double standard

Developer and senior software engineer at Fanatics, Yordis Prieto sharpens that point, writing in reply that Vercel had “invented” OIDC federation yet still left him leaning on “a long-lived access token” in his CI pipeline, and he presses the company to drop the token requirement from GitHub CI while criticizing its non-expiring token option.

Vercel’s GitHub Actions deployment guide still instructs developers to authenticate deployments with a VERCEL_TOKEN secret, and in Thursday’s announcement Ubl says the company is extending OIDC support across its API and CLI to retire long-lived tokens from deployment workflows, which for now leaves Vercel asking Marketplace vendors to adopt a standard its own deployment tooling has not fully implemented.

By November 30, Marketplace integrations that fall short of Vercel’s authentication requirements will carry a “Not secure” warning on their listing, and the company has not published its survey methodology, named the companies it surveyed, or disclosed how many existing Marketplace partners will have to change their authentication systems.

Short-lived tokens for agents

As AI agents gain access to more external services, credential management is becoming a greater consideration for agent harnesses. One way to reduce the risks of persistent access keys is to use short-lived, just-in-time credentials that expire rather than leaving agents with ongoing access.

As AI agents gain access to more external services, credential management is becoming a greater consideration for agent harnesses.

Vercel’s Connect service addresses part of that problem by letting applications and agents request scoped credentials at runtime using their deployment identity rather than storing secrets in application environments. Connect also handles token exchange and renewal.

An October 15 update added enterprise-managed authorization in public beta, allowing administrators to control access to supported services through identity providers such as Okta.

Connect still allows static keys

Even so, Vercel Connect still supports static API keys for providers that lack OAuth or another identity-based option, and its documentation describes storing those credentials centrally and pulling them at runtime, while the underlying keys can still live indefinitely.

The company also introduced GitHub OIDC authentication for its Container Registry in late September, though that work does nothing to remove the VERCEL_TOKEN requirement from its documented GitHub Actions deployment flow.

OIDC across Vercel’s own tooling

For now, Vercel faces the same job it is handing its Marketplace vendors: replacing long-lived credentials across infrastructure it already runs, and until OIDC support reaches workflows like GitHub Actions deployments, developers will keep needing the very tokens Vercel is urging the rest of the industry to give up.

item.title: AI jobs are waiting while GPUs sit idle. Kubernetes has a new plan.
item.dc:creator: Nick Lucchesi
item.description:
Welcome to another edition of Road to KubeCon! We’re tracking movements in the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem as we count

The post AI jobs are waiting while GPUs sit idle. Kubernetes has a new plan. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to another edition of Road to KubeCon! We’re tracking movements in the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem as we count down to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 November 9–12 in Salt Lake City.

Half of our column this week focuses on untangling Kubernetes as we add the demands of agentic AI: automating pod-restart troubleshooting, syncing communication between the scheduler and autoscaler, and maturing how we distribute inference across a cloud-native stack.

The other half goes deeper into what we need to look at closely in Kubernetes environments: What context’s missing, what slips through the gaps in metrics, and whether the AI agents you already use are really worth their salt as SREs.

Let’s get into it.

HPE on automating pod restarts in AI development

As more enterprises turn to Kubernetes for large-scale AI and machine learning jobs, they’re hitting a common obstacle: pod restarts. This is something that HPE has noticed as customers utilize its HPE Private Cloud AI (PCAI) to host long-running AI/ML workloads on inherently ephemeral container-based infrastructure like Kubernetes.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is a presenting sponsor of Road to KubeCon. HPE Software helps IT organizations modernize infrastructure, streamline operations, and accelerate AI initiatives across hybrid, multi-vendor environments.

According to HPE system software engineer Guoping Jia, Kubernetes provides some troubleshooting commands out of the box, but it still requires extensive manual investigation. “This operational workflow does not scale effectively in PCAI’s large-cluster environment,” writes Jia on the HPE blog.

His solution involves smarter automation for troubleshooting, using an open-source Kubernetes troubleshooting tool, k8s-pod-restart-info-collector, to automatically gather details and send diagnostic information straight to a Slack channel. It’s one helpful strategy to improve usability for Kubernetes operators.

Will the scheduler and autoscaler unite?

There’s been a lot of talk recently about how Kubernetes is evolving to meet AI’s new demands. This week, AWS senior software development managers Sajjan Gundapuneedi and Neelendra Bhandari weighed in with this blog post on how AI is reshaping Kubernetes autoscaling.

The core problem they highlight is friction between the scheduler, which places pods on existing nodes, and the autoscaler, which adds new ones, when managing GPU accelerators on Kubernetes. Often the two sides aren’t on the same page, leaving pods pending and pricey GPUs sitting idle. Capacity reservations, device topology, and GPU sharing complicate things further.

“A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it.”

“A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it,” the authors write. “Inference is what makes this pressing rather than academic, since bursty serving and agentic workloads have no patience for a cold node.”

To them, solutions are already taking shape: dynamic resource allocation (DRA)-aware autoscalers, workload-aware scheduling, and a companion mechanism, provisioning requests, to bridge the two sides. Still, they expect the autoscaler to grow into “a more scheduler-aware partner.”

Deeper integration is underway, too. A public proposal in the SIG-Autoscaling group sketches APIs that would let the two loops talk directly, so the scheduler could see capacity that could be provisioned, express placement preferences across it, and request it explicitly.

Distributed AI inference grows up with llm-d v1.0 release

On Tuesday, at PyTorch Conference North America, the CNCF sandbox project llm-d reached v1.0. The project now bridges AI application developers in the PyTorch ecosystem and the production cloud-native stack.

Carlos Costa, co-founder and lead maintainer of llm-d, and a distinguished engineer on IBM’s hybrid cloud platform for AI, says the v1.0 release signals maturity.

“This is the moment open source AI serving crosses from experimental projects into dependable infrastructure you can build on,” Costa tells The New Stack. Whereas earlier versions focused on proving state-of-the-art performance, v1.0 is about sustaining that performance in production, he adds.

llm-d has already seen plenty of use at Tesla, AWS, Oracle, Google, and beyond. Costa adds that a recent IBM Research demonstration found that an agent factory exploring quantum error correction hardware ran at 11.5x lower inference cost on open models with llm-d than on an all-proprietary configuration.

“This demonstration shows where llm-d really shines: agentic workloads,” he says, adding that it absorbs bursty agentic traffic and, in IBM’s test, pushed cache reuse to about 98%.

From building models to operating frontier intelligence at scale

For a taste of the type of discussion to expect at KubeCon NA, let’s briefly visit the East. Chris Aniszczyk, CTO at CNCF, set the stage very well at last month’s KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China 2026 in Shanghai, in the talk Operating Frontier Intelligence at Scale with Xiao Zhang.

As he puts it, it’s not just about models anymore. It’s about putting them all to work. “AI is essentially moving from just purely about building the greatest models [to] how do we actually make this run at scale, stitch it all together and run in different types of environments,” says Aniszczyk.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince recently declared that bot traffic, driven by AI agents, has passed human traffic online for the first time. Aniszczyk says that shift is putting tremendous pressure on systems, pointing to recent GitHub outages. As inference becomes the predominant workload, everything shifts.

“It’s the craziest kind of technology change that I’ve seen probably in my career.”

This shift is causing all sorts of side problems, he notes, from building new infrastructure to building more data centers to ensuring enough power is available. “It’s the craziest kind of technology change that I’ve seen probably in my career,” says Aniszczyk.

Still, he’s an optimist, framing it as a fun problem and challenge for the cloud-native community to tackle together.

Promoting your AI agent to the SRE role

Plenty of AI site reliability engineer (SRE) platforms are emerging. But according to Roy Libman, CPO, Radar (Skyhook.io), your next SRE hire might be right under your fingertips: the AI coding agent you already use. The trick is giving it the right context.

“The coding agent your engineers use, whether that’s Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, can already investigate a Kubernetes cluster,” writes Libman on the CNCF blog. “What it usually lacks is context: what’s failing right now, and what changed before it broke.”

In his benchmark of 50 injected faults on a live cluster, Claude Code, given read-only context through MCP tools, diagnosed slightly more accurately than with shell and kubectl access. The bigger difference was speed: with context, it reached a correct diagnosis within two minutes on 86% of faults, versus 60% with a shell.

It’s an interesting sign that context is king for diagnosing complex errors, and that you might not need to shell (pun intended) out for another AI subscription just to triage issues.

Industry take: what goes undetected in Kubernetes

A previous Road to KubeCon asked what’s still missing with OTel and Prometheus. Well, one gap is state that isn’t a time series, like slowlog entries, client lists, and access control list (ACL) changes, shares Kristiyan Ivanov, former engineering manager at Redis, current contributor to Valkey, and founding CTO of BetterDB. “These get lost between scrapes,” he tells The New Stack.

“Metrics count, but they don’t explain.”

Metrics count, but they don’t explain.” According to Ivanov, much goes undetected in Kubernetes because Valkey and Redis keep evidence in in-memory buffers, which Prometheus reduces to lengths and counters. “Kubernetes makes this even worse in several ways,” he says, noting that pod restarts, failovers, and ephemeral pod IPs worsen tracking.

“Almost everything in the ecosystem is an INFO scraper,” he says. “Missing across the board: durable history across restarts and failovers, attribution to a service or ACL user, an audit trail of ACL and config changes, and aggregation across shards.”

Emerging approaches are helping cloud operators see these gaps. He points to improvements in Valkey’s detection capabilities and OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation to enable granular tracing. But eBPF can’t see evictions, ACL denials, or configuration changes, he says. Those require engine-level collection.

As Kubernetes evolves, so do the demands on the teams running it. Presenting sponsor HPE helps teams address that complexity with software spanning virtualization, cloud management, observability, and automation.

Half can’t measure AI agents effectively

Eighty-seven percent of respondents say monitoring AI is a priority, yet over half admit they can’t effectively measure AI quality, like LLM response quality, or control AI costs, found Splunk State of Observability 2026, which surveyed 2,050 ITOps and engineering professionals and was released Oct. 20.

The report also found 83% are concerned about the unintended consequences of AI agents. This tracks with agentic AI’s tendency to take unexpected actions and create bursty traffic patterns, both of which are driving major infrastructure changes.

“Most companies will soon have far more agents at work than people,” said Jeetu Patel, president and chief product officer at Cisco, in the press release. Monitoring AI is also driving more collaboration between observability and security teams, according to 81% of respondents.

More updates from the cloud-native universe

The excitement around cloud native never sleeps. Here are a few more community, project, and vendor updates from the past week or so.

  • Congratulations to Anish Bista, the first Golden Kubestronaut from Nepal!
  • Kubernetes v1.38.0 is targeted for release on Wednesday, December 16.
  • Per the release schedule, Kubernetes 1.34 hits end of life October 27.
  • Fairwinds shares lessons from running n8n in production on Amazon EKS.
  • Broadcom’s AAI v26 adds cost tracking and Kubernetes support; see EMA’s impact brief.
  • Splunk now lets teams remotely configure OpenTelemetry Collectors on Kubernetes.
  • New Relic shipped v4.8.2 of its Kubernetes integration with dependency updates.

One more stop on the Road to KubeCon

Road to KubeCon is an eight-part series presented by HPE. Before you go, explore how HPE Software helps IT teams do more with less complexity.

This series is almost over — only one edition remains.

We’ll be here next week to round things off with a special sign-off for Road to KubeCon. In the meantime, you can catch up on previous editions in the Road to KubeCon archive.

Bill Doerrfeld, the writer of this series, is open to community pitches. Feel free to share interesting takes, new releases, or tips on the best dive bar in Salt Lake City.

He accepts direct messages on LinkedIn, or you can reach him through his personal contact page.

item.title: PHP2Shell was only the beginning: AI is accelerating the patch race
item.dc:creator: Matthew Weier O’Phinney
item.description:
Government websites and public services across Europe went offline this week as organizations responded to two newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities.

The post PHP2Shell was only the beginning: AI is accelerating the patch race appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Government websites and public services across Europe went offline this week as organizations responded to two newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. Germany took several federal websites offline, France temporarily shut down prefecture sites, Belgium’s foreign ministry disabled its websites, and organizations in the Netherlands pulled public-facing services as a precaution. It wasn’t confined to Europe, with countless other entities and businesses worldwide responding similarly.

They were all waiting for a PHP vulnerability mitigation that didn’t exist yet.

The cause was PHP2Shell: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. While the community worked quickly and the PHP project released fixes for all community-supported PHP versions on the morning of October 21, the bigger issue remains unresolved: an estimated 40% of PHP users are running unsupported PHP, even as AI has exponentially accelerated CVE discovery.

“What happened this week was different, and it’s the first shot of what promises to be an ongoing battle across the open-source ecosystem.”

I’ve been contributing to open source for more than 20 years; I lead the Laminas Project, I’m the Principal Product Manager for Perforce Zend and OpenLogic, and I currently serve on the Board of the PHP Foundation — which is all to say, I’ve seen more than my fair share of new security threats.

What happened this week was different, and it’s the first shot of what promises to be an ongoing battle across the open-source ecosystem.

What you need to know about PHP2Shell

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, currently referred to as PHP2Shell, present remote code execution (RCE) risks triggered by a combination of out-of-memory (OOM) conditions and PHP’s error handling. Every PHP version back to 5.4 is affected by at least one. The two vulnerabilities are particularly concerning because they exist in PHP itself rather than in an individual application, CMS, or framework; there is no real mitigation outside patched PHP runtimes.

Wiz Research found that the vulnerabilities could allow attackers to remotely execute code or expose sensitive information in process memory, including passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates. This exposure exists independently of the application running on PHP.

Additionally, Datadog Security Labs, which independently reproduced the vulnerabilities, found that application-level authentication cannot prevent the attack because PHP processes the malicious request before application code runs. In its reproduction of CVE-2026-109618, researchers reported that the request “never reaches the target application’s code.”

“Even with solid application security practices, your applications could still be exposed because the vulnerable behavior happens below the application, in the PHP runtime itself.”

This means that even with solid application security practices, your applications could still be exposed because the vulnerable behavior happens below the application, in the PHP runtime itself.

The answer is to patch.

The community takes a collaborative effort

Once the full impact became clear in August, the PHP Ecosystem Security Team, the PHP Foundation, and release managers delivered a fix across every supported PHP version. In a cross-ecosystem effort, they also worked with LTS vendors (such as Zend) to ensure they created and released all patches simultaneously.

This is the first time in 20+ years I’ve seen an effort like this happen, and I applaud the community for moving in this direction. Because of this initiative, anyone on a PHP version no longer supported by the community (8.1 or older) could remain secure against these newly disclosed CVEs without any gaps.

Unfortunately, this kind of cooperation also depends on trust, which was tested here. The CVE numbers were leaked on October 20, moving all releases up by a day. But as of 14:00 UTC on October 21, all community-supported PHP versions have received updates to mitigate these vulnerabilities. My team at Zend, along with other LTS providers, also released patches for EOL PHP versions.

While we’ll need more comprehensive steps in the coming weeks, these mitigations will keep critical applications that power governments, hospitals, financial institutions, schools, and more secure and supported in the interim.

AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research

PHP2Shell is a prime example of what happens when AI makes difficult security research more accessible — and the dangers that come with that knowledge.

As part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, Calif identified a critical PHP flaw using GPT-5.6 Sol. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with researchers and security providers contributing testing, technical support, and coordination ahead of disclosure.

“We’ve always raced vulnerability disclosure, patch availability, and exploitation. PHP2Shell demonstrates just how uncomfortable and hard-won that race can, and likely will, become.”

What stands out is the potential shift in scale. OpenAI says these are already among several significant vulnerabilities it has found and is working to address, and it expects similar findings to “increase sharply in the coming months.”

We’ve always raced vulnerability disclosure, patch availability, and exploitation. PHP2Shell demonstrates just how uncomfortable and hard-won that race can, and likely will, become.

Running EOL OSS? AI is raising the stakes.

The easy advice after a vulnerability like PHP2Shell is to upgrade immediately. The operational reality is more complicated.

PHP 8.1 and older releases no longer receive updates from the PHP project, although some distributions and long-term support vendors provide backported security fixes. For critical applications, moving to a new runtime can require updates to frameworks, libraries, extensions, and application code, plus the testing needed to ensure those changes don’t disrupt production.

That gap grows as AI improves vulnerability research, so this isn’t just a PHP issue. PHP is just the first major example of what’s coming for most popular OSS technologies. For instance, we’ve seen a recent flood of Spring vulnerability reports in the past few months, and Node.js and Python reported critical vulnerabilities the same day PHP2Shell landed. I’d also be remiss not to mention Linus Torvalds’ recent comments that the Linux security list is becoming unmanageable because of AI bug reports.

During my time working with OSS and PHP at Perforce Software, I’ve come to view LTS as a bridge to modernization. It lets teams keep addressing security vulnerabilities while they plan, test, and execute a move to a supported version. And, as vulnerability discovery accelerates, remaining indefinitely on unsupported software becomes increasingly difficult to justify.

Organizations need to stay current where they can and have a deliberate security strategy for the systems they can’t upgrade immediately. The faster vulnerabilities are discovered, the more important this will become.

What happens now?

For PHP users, the immediate priority is straightforward: move to a fixed release or obtain appropriate security fixes for an otherwise unsupported version. But let’s talk more long-term.

It can be tempting to use PHP2Shell as evidence that PHP is suddenly less secure, but that couldn’t be further from the truth. The combined community and vendor effort this week proves that. Instead, we need to change our outlook on security, because vulnerabilities like these will only become more common.

“Yes, our capacity to find difficult security problems has improved. But our ability to respond needs to keep pace.”

AI is changing which security investigations are practical and how quickly they can happen. That’s valuable when researchers are working with projects and the wider ecosystem to resolve vulnerabilities. But it also puts more pressure on organizations to know what they’re running, stay on supported releases when possible, establish clear vulnerability-response processes, and have a plan for applications that cannot be upgraded immediately.

Yes, our capacity to find difficult security problems has improved. But our ability to respond needs to keep pace.

The post PHP2Shell was only the beginning: AI is accelerating the patch race appeared first on The New Stack.
AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery. PHP2Shell proves that legacy runtimes can no longer survive without a proactive patch strategy.

item.title: A few engineers asked IT for Linux. Then it spread to 200 machines.
item.dc:creator: David Eastman
item.description:
Linux is already part of the AI developer’s desktop toolkit. Nvidia’s DGX Spark, which became available to order on October

The post A few engineers asked IT for Linux. Then it spread to 200 machines. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Linux is already part of the AI developer’s desktop toolkit. Nvidia’s DGX Spark, which became available to order on October 15, 2025, runs the Ubuntu-based DGX OS. OpenAI’s Codex CLI already supports Linux, another example of AI tools meeting developers where they work.

There’s just one problem. Developers can fall in love with Linux at home. Getting enterprise IT to let them use it at work is another matter.

Angelo Huang, founder and CEO of Swif.ai, a platform that manages and secures employee devices, wants to change that. Huang tells The New Stack that giving developers Linux machines starts with giving IT teams the controls to manage and secure them.

Huang says that starting this past week, Swif began expanding its Linux device management and compliance capabilities, adding Omarchy and Linux Mint support to its roster. Swif is also optimizing the onboarding process across supported Mac, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android environments. They claim that it now takes under 10 minutes to set up device compliance standards such as SOC 2, ISO 27001, and HIPAA.

“Linux already runs much of the infrastructure behind AI,” Huang says. “Increasingly, developers want it on their desks too. The problem isn’t that Linux can’t be secure. It’s that enterprise IT needs to be able to manage it, enforce controls, and prove those controls are working for their compliance requirements. That’s the gap we’re closing.”

“The problem isn’t that Linux can’t be secure. It’s that enterprise IT needs to be able to manage it, enforce controls, and prove those controls are working…”

Swif lists support for Linux distributions including Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, openSUSE, Arch Linux, Manjaro, MX Linux, Pop!_OS, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, NixOS, and Universal Blue.

According to Swif’s Omarchy guide, the tested configuration (version 4.0.2) for x86_64 machines supports device enrollment, inventory tracking, application blocking, and selected OpenClaw logging and tool policies. (The guide flags limitations around login, home encryption, remote desktop, and updates.)

Linux Mint’s status is less straightforward, though.

“Linux Mint works today because it’s built on Ubuntu, and we have customers running it,” Huang says, “but it isn’t on our officially supported list yet. Requests for new distributions come in through support tickets and our customer success team. A customer with a real deployment, the number of seats involved, and how far it diverges from a distribution we already support move a distribution up the priority list. For an Ubuntu- or Fedora-based distribution, initial support typically takes one to two weeks.”

Swif’s software-management guide lists Mint for APT-based application installation, although its Linux enrollment list does not name Mint. That documents a specific capability, rather than full validation of every management policy.

Mint also offers a Debian-based edition, LMDE; shared ancestry alone does not establish compatibility across editions and versions.

Making Linux manageable for enterprise IT

Swif’s Linux management capabilities cover familiar IT needs: policy enforcement, LUKS encryption recovery, and automated remediation. Support varies by distribution and policy; the recovery policy manages access to an already encrypted disk rather than encrypting an unencrypted one.

Swif sends Linux device evidence to the governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) platform Vanta hourly.

It also offers a Drata integration with hourly syncing. Still, Swif’s Drata guide is inconsistent on Linux: it lists Linux evidence fields, but its device eligibility list names only macOS and Windows. Linux teams should confirm Drata coverage with Swif before relying on it.

These records support compliance assessments; they do not, by themselves, establish compliance.

The New Stack asks how a developer might, for example, run Wayland on a Framework laptop, and how this leaves IT to determine which management functions work with that setup.

“Our agent runs in user space and relies mainly on systemd, the package manager, and standard kernel interfaces, so hardware like a Framework laptop is rarely the issue,” Huang says. “The display server is where it gets interesting. Wayland support through PipeWire and xdg-desktop-portal is in development. Our rule of thumb: if it affects whether our agent can enforce policy, report inventory, or prove compliance, it’s ours to fix.”

User space does not mean unprivileged: Swif’s Linux management commands can run as root. PipeWire and desktop portals handle functions like screen sharing; this is distinct from basic device inventory or policy enforcement. Swif’s Omarchy guide flags its RustDesk-based remote desktop policy as having experimental Wayland support.

Let the developers have Linux

“The argument inside companies doesn’t need to be Mac versus Windows versus Linux,” says Huang. “If your AI team wants Linux, the answer from IT shouldn’t automatically be no. Give developers the tools they want to get the job done. Give security the controls it needs.”

“If your AI team wants Linux, the answer from IT shouldn’t automatically be no.”

Swif focuses on enterprise IT, but developers also have a stake in how IT manages their machines. The New Stack asked if it ran a Linux development community.

“The usual story is that a few engineers ask IT to get off Windows, and it grows to 50, 100, sometimes 200. IT then needs a way to manage those machines that a GRC platform will accept as evidence, and that’s when they come to us. We also hear from developers directly, through shared Slack channels with customers, onboarding calls during rollouts, and support tickets filed by end users. We don’t run a community for Linux developers today, but it’s a good idea.”

AI oversight: Documented features and roadmap

“Right now,” Huang says, “we have MCP server management, agentic security, Claude Compliance integration, and Data loss prevention in beta. On the roadmap is integration with OpenAI’s compliance API and agentic compliance.”

After enrolling a Linux machine, Swif’s MDM agent is installed for device management, while installing the Agentic Security agent provides visibility into supported AI-agent activity.

Its Claude compliance integration collects organization-level audit events, while its documented DLP beta uses a browser extension and requires organization-level beta opt-in.

Its email documentation covers Gmail and Outlook on the web, excluding native desktop mail clients. Those features have a different scope than monitoring local agent activity.

“It’s bringing oversight of AI agents on employee endpoints into the device management layer. The problem is simple. Agents run on employee endpoints with access to code, credentials, and customer data, and almost nobody oversees them.

“Agents run on employee endpoints with access to code, credentials, and customer data, and almost nobody oversees them.”

“When OpenClaw first launched, many customers asked us to block it outright. As more people use agents at work, companies have too much to lose from a data breach or IP theft to leave that unmanaged,” Huang says.

OpenClaw’s own security documentation warns that untrusted content can carry prompt injections. The risk depends on the agent’s permissions, tools, and isolation.
