Swif.ai is expanding Linux device management so IT can say yes to developers. The pitch: AI teams get Linux, and security gets proof of control.

item.title: Microsoft’s new voice AI can start working out what you want before you finish speaking
item.dc:creator: Adrian Bridgwater
item.description:
“I think you said, ‘representative.’” It’s the fastest way to bypass automated speech recognition chatbots that fail to route human

The post Microsoft’s new voice AI can start working out what you want before you finish speaking appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
“I think you said, ‘representative.’” It’s the fastest way to bypass automated speech recognition chatbots that fail to route human callers to the service they need. Achieving a human handoff to a living, breathing representative still feels like a badge of honor.

Microsoft wants to change that dynamic.

Naomi Moneypenny, senior director of product development at Microsoft Foundry Models division, blogged on October 1 to introduce three new Microsoft AI (MAI) models in Microsoft Foundry, Redmond’s app and agent model catalog and platform.

“A voice agent has to do more than hear a request and produce a reply. It has to keep the interaction moving while it listens, reasons, uses tools, and speaks. A delay at either end can turn a conversation into a series of awkward pauses,” writes Moneypenny.

Available now in Microsoft Foundry, the latest voice-centric models include MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming, which turns live speech into text as it is spoken; MAI-Voice-2.1, an expressive multilingual text-to-speech model; and MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash, optimized for responsive, high-volume voice applications.

Partials drive incremental speech recognition

Instead of waiting for a person to finish speaking before returning text, the technology (which has automatic language detection) produces its first hypotheses (known as partials, associated with the field of incremental speech recognition) within the “low hundreds of milliseconds” of receiving audio. The model then refines the partials as more context arrives, before committing to a stable transcript once an utterance ends.

“A live transcription experience can surface words almost as quickly as they are spoken.”

“That distinction matters when an application needs to act while someone is speaking. A customer-service agent can begin identifying a caller’s request before the sentence is complete. A voice assistant can start reasoning or preparing a tool call sooner. A live transcription experience can surface words almost as quickly as they are spoken,” writes Moneypenny. 

MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash is proposed as “a natural fit” for live support agents, voice assistants, and other applications that generate spoken responses. Moneypenny suggests developers can choose MAI-Voice-2.1 when “expressive fidelity” is the priority, or Flash when they need to balance natural speech with responsiveness and cost at scale.

Moneypenny is bullish about the benchmarks thus far. Her post noted that MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming “debuts at #1 for accuracy” on both partial and final transcripts on the benchmark-based Artificial Analysis leaderboard. 

Time for voice to speak up?

All said and done then (pun intended), does this mean that across the spectrum of human-machine input methods, voice is now ready for wider use and adoption? CEO of voice-agent platform company Phonely, Will Bodewes, tells The New Stack he sees these developments positively.

“Voice AI is ready for prime time, if Microsoft’s entry into the market is any indication,” Bodewes says.

Microsoft is hardly new to speech, though: Azure Speech has been on the market for years, and it ships the new MAI models. “For an AI developer, that’s an opportunity to build on that momentum, so expect more players to follow suit. But the model is only the beginning. Voice agents need to learn from every call and measurably improve over time. For companies to see real results, their voice AI must be ready for prime time in theory and in practice.”

“In the early days, a speech request to a hosted model could sit behind a thousand others for 30 seconds, which, on a phone call, is a hang-up.”

From an infrastructure-operations perspective, there’s a clear advancement here. Bodewes, whose company builds its own voice-agent LLM, notes that in the early days (and he means back from the mid 2010s onwards in the initial cloud-based speech API era, such as the Google Cloud Speech-to-Text API, Azure Speech Services, Amazon Transcribe, etc.) a speech request to a hosted model could sit behind a thousand others for 30 seconds, which, on a phone call, is a hang-up. 

“We built routing infrastructure just to find the least-loaded endpoints. Owning the model meant owning the queue, and that’s how we got to 120-millisecond responses,” explains Bodewes. “Every sentence you add to a prompt adds another chance of failure. So we enforce the critical steps in code. If an agent needs a name, email, and date of birth before it issues a refund, the codebase guarantees it. Leaving that to the LLM is how you ship incidents.”

The front end (speech) isn’t the hard part

Phonely machine learning researcher Amit Kiran Rege tells The New Stack he agrees the developments are positive, but warns of deeper nuances (speech pun intended, again) in the wider rollout. 

“Microsoft shipped the two ends of the voice agent pipeline, speech in and speech out, which tells you it’s betting on a cascade effect for contact centers, the same as we did. But in our work, we found the ends aren’t the hard part. The hard part is the silence in the middle where the model is deciding whether a caller is done or taking a breath before the next word,” explains Rege.

What surprised Phonely when scaling this type of service to millions of calls is that speeding up the data pipeline makes the agent interrupt callers more. 

“Microsoft shipped the two ends of the voice agent pipeline, speech in and speech out … But in our work, we found the ends aren’t the hard part.”

“Two-thirds of the time our agent decided to jump in too early, and nobody heard it, because the caller resumed before the first syllable and we canceled the reply. Cut your latency in half, and those become audible interruptions. Thus, the lesson is that latency and turn-taking have to improve together,” cautions Rege.

Talking our way into future interfaces

Microsoft’s position on these technologies states that developers can embrace these same models and toolsets to build customer-service agents, multilingual assistants that recognize a spoken language and reply in a consistent voice, what it defines as “interactive learning experiences that move between languages, speakers, and conversational exercises” and live captions and voice-driven interfaces.

The post Microsoft’s new voice AI can start working out what you want before you finish speaking appeared first on The New Stack.
Microsoft’s speech model starts transcribing before callers finish talking. But Phonely says the hard part of voice AI is the silence in the middle.

item.title: Five AI agent harnesses took the same memory test. The results weren’t even close.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
AI agents are getting better at remembering past conversations and earlier tasks but remembering something doesn’t guarantee an agent can

The post Five AI agent harnesses took the same memory test. The results weren’t even close. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI agents are getting better at remembering past conversations and earlier tasks but remembering something doesn’t guarantee an agent can use it to do better work next time. Letta’s new FrontierMemory benchmark, released Wednesday, tests that gap by measuring whether agents can learn from experience rather than by just retrieving stored information. Early results show a widespread in performance across agent harnesses, the the infrastructure that manages how an agent operates.

Letta Dream came out on top with a 73.3% score, followed by Prime Agent at 60%. OpenAI Agents SDK scored 40%, while Claude Managed Agents and Hermes Agent trailed at 33.3% and 26.7%, respectively.

Recall isn’t learning

“Modern ‘memory’ benchmarks are saturated since they measure recall of facts,” Letta co-founder and CEO Charles Packer writes on X, saying that in the coding harness and bash loop era, recall is solved, while continual learning in token space, meaning learning through the context an agent keeps rather than through weight updates, remains unsolved.

Sarah Wooders, also a Letta co-founder, points to another problem on X. Most coding and knowledge-work benchmarks evaluate unrelated tasks with all the necessary context provided upfront. But that’s not how people actually work. Wooders compares it to starting a new job: A new hire needs plenty of direction, while someone who’s been there for years can often get the job done with little explanation.

Packer’s premise is that “if AI-generated memory is good, it should actually improve downstream task performance.”

FrontierMemory takes a different approach. Agents receive transcripts of earlier work, including successful and failed attempts, and then generate their own memories to help complete later tasks. Packer’s premise is that “if AI-generated memory is good, it should actually improve downstream task performance.” Developers have already embraced the underlying idea, building continually learning agents by pairing a language model with memory systems and feedback loops.

Letta reworked existing coding and knowledge-work tests so agents had to use what they learned from previous tasks instead of having everything spelled out for them. After reviewing and fixing problems with the original tests, Letta narrowed FrontierMemory 1.0 to just 15 tasks.

Harness beats model

The harness itself may matter just as much as the model running inside it. Letta tested five agent systems to see how well they could learn from previous work and use those lessons on new tasks.

The harness itself may matter just as much as the model running inside it.

Letta Dream beat OpenAI Agents SDK 60% to 40% when both used GPT-6.1 Sol to create memories and GPT-6 Sol to complete tasks. The results were even further apart with Claude Opus 5.5. Dream scored 73.3%, Prime Agent hit 60%, and Claude Managed Agents came in at 33.3%.

Packer says the the way agents handle AI “dreaming” makes a big difference. Dreaming is when an agent reviews past work and turns what it learned into instructions or memories it can use later. He also points to Prime Agent outperforming Hermes Agent as another example of how much these systems can vary. But there’s a downside: without checks on what gets saved, agents risk learning and repeating bad habits.

FrontierMemory also compared seven frontier models on how well they generate useful memories. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 tied for first at 73.3%, Kimi K3 followed at 66.7%, and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol and Google’s Gemini 4 Argon both scored 60%. Muse Wonder reached 46.7%, and Grok 4.7 finished at 33.3%. Packer says Opus 5.5 and GLM-5.3 are significantly better at generating useful memories than GPT-6.1 Sol.

Packer says Opus 5.5 and GLM-5.3 are significantly better at generating useful memories than GPT-6.1 Sol.

Cheaper memory, lower scores

But OpenAI had a big price advantage. GPT-6.1 Sol cost an estimated $0.77 per task, compared with $2.80 for Opus 5.5 and $3.58 for GLM-5.3. So while OpenAI scored lower, it was much cheaper to run.

Letta used its Dream harness to create memories with each model, then tested how well those memories worked on tasks run in Letta Code. The results show a tradeoff between better memory, stronger performance and lower costs.

Memory that travels

Letta also looked at why some memories worked better than others. In one test involving company pricing data, Opus 5.5 created a skill telling the agent when to use certain information. GPT-6.1 Sol created four separate skills, but the agent never found the one it needed.

Gemini 4 Argon made a different mistake. It remembered specific file sizes, which wasn’t much help when the next task involved different files. Opus 5.5 instead told the agent to check both the usual file and email for information. That worked even when the task changed. Memories created by Opus 5.5 helped GPT-6 Sol complete tasks, suggesting developers could use a more expensive model to build memories and a cheaper one to do the work.

Other developers have taken notice. After Letta’s Sarah Wooders posted about the benchmark on X, the OpenClaw account responded that it would like to see a plugin for its platform. The account says its multiplayer environment would be an interesting place to test the benchmark, raising questions about how memory works when several agents share the same harness.

“Yes definitely – would love to add OpenClaw to the harness comparison!” Wooders writes. “Extending to multiplayer memory is also a very interesting future direction.”

What the benchmark misses

FrontierMemory is still early. With just 15 tasks and one attempt per task, a single result can shift the scores by roughly 6.7 percentage points. The benchmark currently focuses on agents learning from past work rather than updating memories as they go. Packer says the next release will add longer-running tasks and online memory updates.

The post Five AI agent harnesses took the same memory test. The results weren’t even close. appeared first on The New Stack.
Letta’s new FrontierMemory benchmark tests whether AI agents learn from experience, and the harness matters as much as the model behind it.

item.title: Ramp built an AI agent harness in six weeks — and LangChain’s CEO says it’s part of a bigger shift
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Ramp spent months testing managed agent APIs, open-source frameworks, and third-party platforms before concluding it would be better off building

The post Ramp built an AI agent harness in six weeks — and LangChain’s CEO says it’s part of a bigger shift appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Ramp spent months testing managed agent APIs, open-source frameworks, and third-party platforms before concluding it would be better off building its own. The result is Laminar, an internal agent harness that took six weeks to reach a first version and now powers every agentic product at the fintech company.

“We studied the other offerings on the market and decided that we could do better, move faster, and have stronger alignment to where we want to go by building in house.”

“We studied the other offerings on the market and decided that we could do better, move faster, and have stronger alignment to where we want to go by building in house,” Sam Kronick, the Ramp engineer behind the platform, writes in the company’s engineering blog.

In Tuesday’s post, Ramp detailed how Laminar brings agent execution, sandboxing, observability, and asynchronous workflows under a single platform. The architecture caught the attention of LangChain CEO Harrison Chase, who praised several design choices in his X post, while pointing to similar work underway in LangChain’s Deep Agents.

Ramp and LangChain are approaching the problem from different directions, but both point to a bigger shift in agent infrastructure. As harnesses take on more responsibility, enterprises have to decide how much of that infrastructure they want to build and maintain themselves.

Why Ramp built in-house

Ramp didn’t want to be locked into one model provider. It needed the flexibility to switch models based on cost, speed, and performance, along with better visibility into how its agents behaved. Engineers were already digging through traces to find unnecessary tool calls, bloated context, and errors, but existing observability tools made that harder than it needed to be. So Ramp built its own debugging interface into Laminar. Keeping development in-house also meant the harness team could work directly with product engineers instead of waiting on vendors to make changes.

Chase agreed with Ramp’s priorities, particularly model independence and observability, both of which LangChain has emphasized in its own work. And, there were other parts of Laminar’s architecture that caught his attention.

Keeping development in-house also meant the harness team could work directly with product engineers instead of waiting on vendors to make changes.

Sessions split from sandboxes

Laminar runs everything from customer service agents to Ramp Inspect, the company’s cloud coding agent, and Glass, which handles longer-running, collaborative work. Supporting these products requires a harness that can manage persistent sessions, human approvals, and work across environments.

Chase highlights Kronick’s observation that a production harness does far more than run a simple execution loop. “+100 to this,” he writes, pointing to LangChain’s investment in Deep Agents.

Ramp keeps agent sessions separate from the sandboxes where code runs. Conversation history and execution state are stored independently, allowing sandboxes to spin up and shut down without disrupting a session.

Chase sees the sandbox-as-a-tool approach as a growing trend, noting that Deep Agents uses a similar design. It also keeps credentials and orchestration outside the sandbox, an important consideration as developers work to isolate agents running untrusted code.

Async agents by default

Laminar lets agents keep working without waiting for every step to finish. Chase describes non-blocking asynchronous agents as the future and says LangChain is developing similar functionality for Deep Agents.

Ramp’s Connectors Service also caught his attention. It centralizes authentication, credentials, access controls, and tool execution behind a shared API.

Chase says LangChain is exploring comparable features for managed Deep Agents. Centralizing those functions also gives platform teams a consistent place to manage access and credential handling rather than implementing them separately for every agent.

The harness is also where teams can trim inference costs, and LangChain has made that case directly. In an October 1 engineering post, it describes moving model selection into the harness of Open SWE, its open-source coding agent. A router examines the initial request and assigns one of three models based on expected task complexity, sending the simplest work to GLM-5.3-Flash, intermediate tasks to GPT-5.6 Sol, and the most demanding requests to GPT-6 Astra.

Routing trims inference costs

Across 973 agent threads, the router cut median LLM costs from $2.61 to $0.94 per thread, a 64 percent drop compared with using GPT-6 Astra for every task. The savings didn’t come with a measurable hit to performance. Merged pull request rates were 29.2 percent for routed threads and 27.3 percent for the control group, a difference that wasn’t statistically significant. Ninety percent of requests went to the two less expensive model tiers.

LangChain argues that routing works better inside the harness than at a generic LLM gateway, where there’s less context about what an agent is doing.

LangChain argues that routing works better inside the harness than at a generic LLM gateway, where there’s less context about what an agent is doing. The harness already knows which prompts, tools, and domain context are involved, giving it more information to make that choice. LangChain uses model-selection middleware to pick a model at the start of each thread.

The results don’t tell us whether building a custom harness is cheaper than using an existing framework. Ramp wasn’t part of the experiment. But they do show how much companies can save by making smarter model choices at the harness level, especially when their agents handle tasks with very different demands.

The harness ownership dilemma

Ramp’s decision also shows how coding agents have changed infrastructure costs. Kronick says agents generated all of Laminar’s initial code, with experienced engineers guiding the architecture and implementation.

But building the first version in six weeks is one thing. Maintaining it is another. Ramp still needs engineers to handle incidents, update the platform, and support its product teams. The company also hasn’t published operating-cost comparisons or benchmarks against competing platforms, which makes it difficult to judge whether building in-house is cheaper.

LangChain offers another option. Rather than building a harness from scratch, companies can use frameworks that handle much of the underlying infrastructure, an approach other vendors are also taking as they open-source their own harnesses.

The post Ramp built an AI agent harness in six weeks — and LangChain’s CEO says it’s part of a bigger shift appeared first on The New Stack.
Ramp built its own AI agent harness, Laminar, instead of buying one. LangChain’s Harrison Chase sees a bigger shift in how agents get built.

item.title: OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
OpenAI on Thursday announced that it is donating the Open Responses API specification to the open source Agentic AI Foundation

The post OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI on Thursday announced that it is donating the Open Responses API specification to the open source Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF).

In addition to Open Responses, OpenSandbox, Anthropic’s Agent Skills, and HuggingFace’s OpenEv framework for agent environments are also joining the AAIF.

The join other AAIF projects like the MCP and A2A protocols, AGENTS.md (also from OpenAI), the open source AI agent goose, agentgateway, and Agent Router. The foundation, which is part of the Linux Foundation, launched in December 2025, with MCP, goose, and AGENTS.md as its first projects.

As for Open Responses, the core idea here is to provide developers with a set of core API calls that should work across LLM providers. When OpenAI first announced the specification in January, the team behind the project noted that virtually all LLM providers now offer the same building blocks (messages, tool calls, function calling, etc.), but that they also all represent them differently in their APIs.

Open Responses aims to create a spec that standardizes these primitives so that developers don’t have to translate between each vendor’s idiosyncratic API when they switch between models.

“When we co-founded AAIF, we contributed AGENTS.md, a way to give coding agents project-specific instructions,” an OpenAI spokesperson told The New Stack. “Open Responses addresses another part of building agents by giving developers a shared format for working with models across endpoints that support it, so they have fewer provider-specific integrations to maintain. Vercel AI Gateway and Databricks Model Serving already implement it, and AAIF will provide a neutral home for developers and providers to continue developing the specification together.”

Why a neutral home matters

It’s this neutral home that is generally the reason why companies donate projects to a foundation. The AAIF is part of the Linux Foundation, which has become somewhat of the de facto standard for providing vendor-neutral homes for popular open source projects, with a technical steering committee, which will initially be made up of project maintainers, handling the technical discussions.

Who already supports it — and who doesn’t

There is already wide support for the spec, with the likes of AWS (in Bedrock), Databricks, LM Studio, Ollama, Hugging Face, Nvidia, OpenRouter, Red Hat, Vercel, and open source projects like vLLM and OGC (previously Llama Stack) supporting it.

Among the names that are missing from this list is OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which defines its own Messages API for giving developers access to its models. Anthropic is a member of the AAIF, so maybe we’ll see the company adopt this spec at some point in the future.

With the Interactions API, Google, too, has its default for letting developers work with its models.

Open Responses doesn’t hide its lineage. The project’s own contributor guide notes that its core schema files are copied from OpenAI’s API. And while OpenAI’s earlier Chat Completions API became an early standard that others used to model their offerings after, Anthropic’s Messages API has now also left a clear mark (in large part thanks to the success of Claude Code), with the likes of DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, and others exposing Anthropic-compatible endpoints, too.

That split is exactly the kind of fragmentation a vendor-neutral spec like this is meant to fix, of course.

The post OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation appeared first on The New Stack.
OpenAI is donating Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation. Here’s who supports it and who’s still missing.

item.title: OpenAI’s COBOL migration score has made a striking leap
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
This week, OpenAI put COBOL in the spotlight. It announced benchmark results suggesting its latest models are getting much better

The post OpenAI’s COBOL migration score has made a striking leap appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
This week, OpenAI put COBOL in the spotlight. It announced benchmark results suggesting its latest models are getting much better at migrating COBOL programs and building software in languages with less code and documentation for models to learn from.

On OpenAI’s own COBOL migration test, GPT-6.1 Sol reached 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, up from GPT-5.6 Sol’s 5.4%, while costing 39% less. At higher reasoning effort, the newer model reached 97.9%.

But the evidence behind the two evaluations is uneven. 

OpenAI has not published the details of its evaluation of COBOL (“Common Business-Oriented Language”; the programming language that AI coding tools may help maintain or migrate). It has released the MultiLangBench setup and test suite on GitHub. That benchmark tests whether models can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 programming languages. 

OpenAI’s announcement calls the results “substantial improvements across both evaluations, delivering much higher accuracy at lower cost.”

Those results could matter to teams maintaining and modernizing legacy software. But without public COBOL test cases, developers cannot independently inspect that evaluation.

Is there finally some hope for modernizing COBOL?

Per OpenAI, its new COBOL migration evaluation “tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior.” Specifically, it’s testing migrations from COBOL to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, and Rust. 

To succeed, each migration must pass a series of hidden tests that require “byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs.” And with markedly greater accuracy than its predecessor, GPT-6.1 Sol is, indeed, showing substantial progress. 

The measured gains are striking, though OpenAI is not the first company to bring AI to COBOL modernization.

Even though COBOL underpins much of the world’s financial transactions and business records — IBM reports COBOL underpins over 40% of all online banking systems, supports 80% of in-person credit card transactions, and handles 95% of all ATM transactions — it remains a difficult target for AI coding tools.

Compared with Python and JavaScript, models have less COBOL code and documentation to learn from. Experienced COBOL developers can also be hard to find, and documentation often lags behind the systems they maintain.

AI coding gains across 20 languages

Alongside its COBOL migration tests, OpenAI developed a second evaluation to measure models’ ability to build software from scratch, MultiLangBench. This benchmark “tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine across 20 different programming languages.” 

First, the program gets a database and SQL query. Then, it produces a modified database. The reference SQLite implementation serves as the ground truth to check if the resulting database contains the expected data. 

On average, GPT-6 Astra — OpenAI’s flagship model — achieved an 87.4% test pass rate across 20 programming languages, a hefty jump from GPT-5.6 Sol’s modest 26.8%. It scored above 83% on 19 out of 20 languages and made improvements on all of them. 

GPT-6 Luna, predictably, didn’t do as well as Astra, with the lower-cost option only achieving an average pass rate of 40.3%. That said, it did manage to outperform GPT-5.6 Sol on every language tested, with an approximate 78% lower estimated API cost. 

All right, then. Keep your secrets.

OpenAI reports promising results from its COBOL migration evaluation and MultiLangBench, but benchmarks don’t tell the whole story. As of Thursday, Real-SWE 1.1, which uses private codebases, lists Claude Opus 5.5 in first place at 56.8% resolution. An earlier Real-SWE run covered by The New Stack had a different leader and lower scores.

Plus, developers still can’t inspect OpenAI’s COBOL migration benchmark. The announcement credits feedback from developers and enterprise customers for guiding the work, but without the underlying tests and dataset, outsiders can’t independently check the results.

OpenAI acknowledges a key limitation, noting that “applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.”

OpenAI is entering a field others have been working on for some time. Anthropic outlined how Claude Code could assist COBOL modernization on February 23. As The New Stack reported, AWS introduced AI agents for mainframe migrations in 2024. 

The post OpenAI’s COBOL migration score has made a striking leap appeared first on The New Stack.
OpenAI reports dramatic improvements in legacy software modernization, but it's keeping the tests behind its biggest claim private.

item.title: Google and AWS open new paths for PyTorch beyond Nvidia
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
At PyTorch Conference North America 2026 this week, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, now available

The post Google and AWS open new paths for PyTorch beyond Nvidia appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
At PyTorch Conference North America 2026 this week, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, now available on GitHub. AWS also launched TorchNeuron in public beta, its open-source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, also available on GitHub.

Both releases seem aimed at making it easier for developers to move beyond Nvidia GPUs, whose CUDA software ecosystem has long dominated AI development. But while Google and AWS’s new offerings do ease some of the challenges of switching hardware, getting top-tier performance still isn’t straightforward. 

For developers eager for more computing options, it’s promising but somewhat disappointing.

Google wants to make TPUs more PyTorch-friendly

Google put TorchTPU in preview with select customers in April (PyTorch says Google’s been working on the project since mid-2025), teasing a simpler way to run PyTorch workloads on Google’s AI chips. PyTorch support has long been an awkward dance, so the new backend could make it easier to run existing models on TPUs.

Google says it wants to make its TPU software ecosystem more open and developer-friendly for the PyTorch community, as it works to make the chips a more practical option for developers already using PyTorch. 

Developed in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta, TorchTPU allows developers to run existing PyTorch workloads without JAX dependencies in the runtime. This way, rather than requiring extensive code changes, developers can migrate existing workloads with only “trivial code changes,” according to PyTorch. 

Specifically, developers can use eager execution to debug models and torch.compile to optimize TPU utilization and reduce memory overhead. 

The new PyTorch stack from Google and Meta comes alongside a slew of other products and integrations announced at the conference, which Google says are “designed to help you run PyTorch effectively on Google Cloud or in your own infrastructure.” Google also announced integrations involving Hugging Face, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray and TorchRec, while contributing LiteRT to the PyTorch ecosystem. 

AWS wants in, too

AWS’s release extends the same PyTorch-native approach to its own AI chips.

Like TorchTPU, TorchNeuron gives developers a way to natively experiment and build models with PyTorch — this time for Trainium, AWS’s portfolio of AI chips designed for deep learning training and inference workloads. The public beta supports Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. 

AWS says moving a model to Trainium can be as simple as switching to .to(‘neuron’) for eager execution. Compiled models also need the Neuron backend selected, either as the default or in a torch.compile call.

TorchNeuron also integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) — a bare-metal language and compiler for programming AWS Trainium and Inferentia NeuronDevices — so developers can create custom operators and optimize performance on Trainium. AWS and PyTorch have published more detailed guidance on the backend’s execution modes and performance tradeoffs.

Both are getting closer, but not there yet

While TorchTPU and TorchNeuron are notable steps forward in opening up more hardware choices for PyTorch developers, neither is a silver bullet.

PyTorch says a simple code change can get models running on TPUs, but peak performance can require TPU-specific optimization.

For distributed workloads, PyTorch says TorchTPU’s default Skinny Collectives approach can incur an end-to-end performance penalty of roughly 30–40% compared with an optimized approach because it prevents the XLA compiler from overlapping computation and communication.

For workloads seeking peak performance, PyTorch recommends additional tuning and production-grade stacks: 

“Of course, for production workloads seeking peak performance we would absolutely recommend pursuing an optimal approach based on Pallas kernels and production-grade stacks such as vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, or TorchTitan-TorchTPU, as examples.”

TorchNeuron is in public beta. In a separate blog post, AWS says teams can try Trainium with a configuration change instead of a code or model rewrite “in most cases,” leaving open which workloads need more changes.

In a case study, AWS describes how its Generative AI Innovation Center worked with AI research and technology company i14 to adapt its Laplace 3B model for Trainium2. The implementation required three changes: 1) using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel; 2) redesigning how Muon communicates; 3) compiling the sequential backward pass.

The releases give PyTorch developers more options beyond Nvidia GPUs. For now, moving existing code is easier than getting peak performance on unfamiliar chips. 

The post Google and AWS open new paths for PyTorch beyond Nvidia appeared first on The New Stack.
Both companies want to make their AI chips more accessible to PyTorch developers. It’s still hard, though.

item.title: AI found a critical PHP flaw. The bigger failure began in 2024.
item.dc:creator: Steven J. Vaughan-Nichols
item.description:
Did one of your favorite websites go dark on Wednesday? Some did, as operators took services offline while they waited

The post AI found a critical PHP flaw. The bigger failure began in 2024. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Did one of your favorite websites go dark on Wednesday? Some did, as operators took services offline while they waited for fixes to two critical flaws in PHP, the language behind much of the web.

The precaution didn’t mean those sites were hacked. The holes themselves were bad news with a capital B. But the bigger long-term concern might be how the embargo on the patches was handled.

PHP powers roughly 70% of websites, but that figure describes PHP’s reach, not the number of vulnerable or compromised sites. 

WordPress told site owners to update PHP; these flaws don’t require a WordPress update. 

The flaws are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The PHP project’s fixed releases are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12; users of older PHP branches need a supported upgrade or a distributor’s backport.

The PHP security emergency, aka PHP2Shell, exposed more than dangerous bugs in a widely used language. The release also set off a dispute over coordinated disclosure and underscored the pressure on open-source maintainers as AI-assisted researchers find and develop exploits faster.

The road to this emergency ran through OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative. Working in that program, security firm Calif used GPT-5.6 Sol to find a route to remote code execution and reported it to PHP on August 11. OpenAI independently reported the same underlying issue that day; Wiz reported its findings on August 24. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes. They had spotted signs of the underlying out-of-memory problem in 2024, but its full impact became clear only this August.

“This is about as broad as a critical vulnerability gets.”

“This is about as broad as a critical vulnerability gets,” Moshe Siman Tov Bustan of OX Security said in a statement. “If you have a publicly accessible PHP instance and haven’t patched it, start from the assumption that you’re exposed. If you find evidence of exploitation, assume compromise, not just exposure.” 

OX Security CEO Neatsun Ziv added: “This is what an internet-scale vulnerability looks like. When a flaw hits technology this ubiquitous, the blast radius isn’t one product or one industry. It’s the web itself.”

Behind those warnings, open-source leaders are debating how the industry should respond when discovery outpaces remediation. The New Stack has reported on the flood of AI-generated vulnerability reports facing maintainers; PHP’s case adds a dispute over whether an embargo still protected users once details began to leak.

A disclosure dispute and an admission of failure

Before the patches were released, details of PHP2Shell began to leak. The PHP Foundation says two CVE IDs circulated on October 20, followed by an accidentally published proof-of-concept video. 

Chainguard CEO and co-founder Dan Lorenc then released patched container images more than six hours before the October 21 coordinated release. He says he believed reports of active exploitation justified the decision to break the embargo.

The speed concern is real: After WordPress released version 7.1.2 on September 22 to fix CVE-2026-87902, Patchstack observed probes against WordPress sites that same day and attempts to write files the next day.

That, by the way, is bad enough. But the WordPress episode doesn’t establish whether attackers successfully exploited these PHP flaws when Chainguard published its images.

Why Lorenc jumped the clock

In an email to The New Stack, later reflected in his LinkedIn post, Lorenc said Chainguard independently discovered the same issue with its testing harness and a frontier AI model prompted to “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP.”

Lorenc said Chainguard first heard on Friday, October 16, that a PHP issue was coming. It independently found the issue that night, received a full briefing on Saturday, October 17, and helped test fixes. 

He said news began leaking Monday, October 19, and discussion intensified Tuesday night, when several vendors reported what they believed were exploits in the wild.

Lorenc wites that, after a video call with other researchers, he decided to ship the fixes and immediately notified the disclosure group. He said he believed the coordinated disclosure guidelines allowed early release when there was evidence of exploitation in the wild.

Lorenc said three considerations drove the decision. These were how easily Chainguard had independently discovered the vulnerability and built an exploit, how much information was already circulating about the vulnerabilities and fixes, and the evidence shared about active exploitation.

Chainguard made its patched images publicly accessible, rather than restricting them to customers. Lorenc acknowledged that the PHP Foundation disagreed with his decision.

They certainly didn’t agree. The PHP Foundation’s account was blunter: “Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix.” It said Chainguard had received the patch early so customers could update at the agreed disclosure time. 

In the foundation’s view, publishing the built images gave attackers a chance to study the fix while other PHP users were still waiting for patches.

“We’re not always going to get it right, and not everyone is going to agree with our decisions.”

Lorenc wrote that he was sorry his decision added stress for PHP’s maintainers. “We’re not always going to get it right, and not everyone is going to agree with our decisions,” he said, adding that Chainguard’s goal was to protect the most people.

What counts as an exploit?

The disagreement centered on what counted as evidence of active exploitation. Lorenc said other vendors had seen exploits in the wild. The PHP Foundation said its security team had not identified a functional exploit among the circulating proofs of concept at the time of release. 

Amazon Threat Intelligence later reported an apparent exploit attempt against one of its honeypots on October 17 and more attempts early on October 21. Still, it said it was unclear whether those attempts would have succeeded on real systems.

The competing risks are clear. Yes, holding an embargo gives distributors time to prepare updates together. And, true, releasing a fix early may protect users who can obtain it. But it also gives attackers clues while other PHP users are still waiting for patches.

The capital-B problem underneath

The PHP Foundation also acknowledged a separate failure in its response. Developers noticed signs of the out-of-memory problem behind one CVE during a 2024 audit, but had not found a concrete route to remote code execution. 

The foundation said competing fixes carried difficult compatibility and security trade-offs, and work repeatedly stalled. It called the delay “a structural failure” caused by its decision process and lack of resources. 

The New Stack has previously reported on the link between paid maintenance and security practices. The foundation is now seeking more support from companies, hosts and governments that depend on PHP.

Canonical, Ubuntu Linux‘s parent company, offers a less critical assessment of the overall response. In an e-mail, Luci Stanescu, Canonical’s security engineering manager, says, “Canonical supports and recommends coordinated vulnerability disclosure according to best practices. The early embargo leak by a third-party was unfortunate, but we believe the disclosure process worked well.”

That assessment differs in emphasis from the PHP Foundation’s criticism: a leak can undermine part of the process without necessarily invalidating the broader coordination effort.

For CIQ Chief Technology Officer Peter Nelson, whose company is Rocky Linux’s founding sponsor, the PHP episode fits a broader change already underway in Linux security. 

“We have seen AI used in exploiting vulnerabilities in the kernel space for the past six months,” Nelson says. “This represents more research going into other widely used software programs like PHP. We expect to see more of it as open-source projects continue to use AI and other means to harden the code and provide a greater defense against vulnerabilities like this.”

“Today, such vulnerability exploitation requires a frontier model. Tomorrow that won’t be the case.”

Nelson expects that pressure to continue as advanced vulnerability-research capabilities become more accessible. “Today, such vulnerability exploitation requires a frontier model. Tomorrow that won’t be the case.”

Lorenc also frames the challenge as an industry-wide problem rather than one confined to PHP. “This is unfortunately the new normal for the industry, and we’re going to need to work together as one team to have a chance at securing our critical infrastructure fast enough to stop attackers from causing real harm.”

Patching cannot wait for the usual maintenance window.

For enterprise users, the immediate consequences are operational. Gunnar Hellekson, Red Hat’s vice president and general manager for Lightwell, a joint Red Hat–IBM effort to address vulnerable open-source dependencies, tells The New Stack in an email that the PHP flaws illustrate the risk in dependable software that organizations may rarely think about.

Hellekson said that stable production software can be easy to overlook even as AI-driven discovery increases the volume and speed of vulnerability findings. The PHP issues, he said, remind us how deeply open source is woven into the systems that run businesses.

He emphasized getting tested updates from trusted suppliers, especially when vulnerabilities affect vital programs like PHP. “Given the potential impact of these vulnerabilities, Red Hat recommends that customers deploy validated, tested patches as soon as they are available from trusted sources including Red Hat, even outside of normal patching windows.”

“Software that supports millions of websites cannot depend on a handful of maintainers to manage increasingly sophisticated threats alone.”

Beyond that, we need more resources, in general, for open-source software maintenance and security. As Kara Sprague, CEO of HackerOne, says in a statement sent to the media, “The PHP discoveries are also a reminder that open-source security is everyone’s responsibility. Software that supports millions of websites cannot depend on a handful of maintainers to manage increasingly sophisticated threats alone.” 

No, no it can’t.

For organizations running affected PHP systems, the “patch it right now!” problem remains: deploy a fixed build and review systems for signs of attempted exploitation, including activity dating back to October 17.

This is where the competing assessments converge. Better-funded maintainers, more resilient disclosure procedures, and broader access to defensive tools could address the longer-term problem. And that’s the capital-B problem underneath this week’s patch.

The post AI found a critical PHP flaw. The bigger failure began in 2024. appeared first on The New Stack.
Two critical PHP flaws sent some sites offline. The fight over Chainguard’s early patch release may outlast the bugs themselves.

item.title: Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership
item.dc:creator: Oladimeji Sowole

The post Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
At 2:07 a.m., an AI agent starts failing. 

The application is still running, but requests are timing out because a downstream API is returning errors. The agent has already retried twice, using more tokens than usual, and its response time has roughly doubled.

The first question should not be:

	“Which model should we use?”

It should be:

	“Who owns this system right now?”

That question is easy to overlook when building AI agents. Teams often pour effort into prompts, retrieval, tools, and model selection, but production ownership determines whether an agent becomes a dependable service or another source of operational risk.

“Teams often pour effort into prompts, retrieval, tools, and model selection, but production ownership determines whether an agent becomes a dependable service or another source of operational risk.”

A production agent needs an owner, boundaries, telemetry, failure policies, escalation paths, and a clear distinction between what the system may automate and what requires human intervention.

A production agent should not have a direct path from reasoning to action. Each tool invocation should pass through explicit controls, remain observable, and have a defined path to human intervention.

Here’s a practical way to build those controls.

Step 1: Treat the agent as a production service

An agent should have the same operational identity as any other production service.

Start by defining its ownership metadata.

Python
from pydantic import BaseModel


class AgentService(BaseModel):
    name: str
    owner_team: str
    service_tier: str
    escalation_channel: str


agent_service = AgentService(
    name="incident-command-agent",
    owner_team="platform-engineering",
    service_tier="critical",
    escalation_channel="#platform-oncall",
)

This may look simple, but it changes the conversation.

The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path.

“The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path.”

You can later attach the same metadata to logs, traces, dashboards, alerts, and deployment records.

Step 2: Define what the agent is allowed to do

Ownership also means being clear about what an agent is allowed to do.

An agent that can only read telemetry carries far less risk than one that can restart production services, change infrastructure, or deploy code.

That’s why I prefer an explicit tool allowlist, which limits the agent to the actions you’ve deliberately granted it.

Python
ALLOWED_TOOLS = {
    "get_service_health",
    "get_recent_deployments",
    "search_runbooks",
    "summarize_incident",
}


class ToolAuthorizationError(Exception):
    """Raised when an agent attempts to use an unapproved tool."""


def authorize_tool(tool_name: str) -> None:
    if tool_name not in ALLOWED_TOOLS:
        raise ToolAuthorizationError(
            f"Tool '{tool_name}' is not authorized."
        )

The guiding principle is deny by default.

Adding a new capability should be an intentional engineering decision, not something that happens because a tool became available to the agent.

For destructive operations, authorisation should be even stricter. A production restart or deployment should require authenticated human approval, not the agent’s own judgment.

Step 3: Put budgets around agent execution

An agent that can reason indefinitely is difficult to operate.

Every production workflow should have limits around execution time, model calls, tool calls, and ideally token consumption.

Python
import os


class ExecutionBudget:
    def __init__(
        self,
        max_steps: int | None = None,
        max_tools: int | None = None,
    ):
        self.steps = 0
        self.tool_calls = 0

        self.max_steps = (
            max_steps
            if max_steps is not None
            else int(os.getenv("MAX_AGENT_STEPS", "5"))
        )

        self.max_tools = (
            max_tools
            if max_tools is not None
            else int(os.getenv("MAX_TOOL_CALLS", "8"))
        )

        if self.max_steps <= 0 or self.max_tools <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                "Execution budget limits must be positive."
            )

    def check_step(self) -> None:
        if self.steps >= self.max_steps:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Agent step budget exceeded."
            )

        self.steps += 1

    def check_tool_call(self) -> None:
        if self.tool_calls >= self.max_tools:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Agent tool-call budget exceeded."
            )

        self.tool_calls += 1

Execution limits should be configurable rather than buried in application code. By passing these limits through the constructor, engineers can assign different budgets to different agents without changing global settings. A diagnostic agent might need only three steps, while a more complex research workflow may require considerably more. When no limits are supplied, the class falls back to environment variables. What matters is that every workflow has a defined ceiling, and that the same budget is enforced throughout its execution.

Step 4: Make model calls observable

An owner cannot operate what they cannot see.

At minimum, record:

  • request latency;
  • model used;
  • success/failure;
  • tool calls;
  • token usage where available;
  • correlation or request ID;
  • escalation events.

A simple wrapper provides a useful boundary.

Python
import logging
import time
import uuid

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def invoke_model(model, messages):
    request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    started = time.perf_counter()

    # Extract the model name across different provider libraries.
    model_name = (
        getattr(model, "model_name", None)
        or getattr(model, "model", None)
        or "unknown_model"
    )

    try:
        response = model.invoke(messages)

        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started

        logger.info(
            "agent_model_call_success",
            extra={
                "request_id": request_id,
                "model": model_name,
                "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3),
            },
        )

        return response

    except Exception:
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started

        logger.exception(
            "agent_model_call_failed",
            extra={
                "request_id": request_id,
                "model": model_name,
                "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3),
            },
        )

        raise

The request ID becomes especially valuable when an incident involves several services.

An engineer should be able to move from an alert to the agent request and then to the underlying model and tool calls.

In production, supplement this logging layer with distributed tracing and metrics for a more complete view of system behaviour and performance.

Step 5: Separate failure from escalation

A failed model call does not necessarily mean the entire service should fail.

Likewise, a successful model call does not mean the agent’s recommendation should execute automatically.

These are different decisions.

Python
def handle_agent_failure(error: Exception) -> dict:
    logger.error(
        "Agent execution failed; escalating to human.",
        exc_info=(
            type(error),
            error,
            error.__traceback__,
        ),
    )

    return {
        "status": "escalated",
        "message": (
            "The AI agent could not complete the operation. "
            "Human intervention is required."
        ),
        "error_type": type(error).__name__,
    }

This distinction matters during a real incident.

The agent might go down, but the engineering team should still be able to respond using the underlying workflows and runbooks. That is what graceful degradation looks like in practice.

Step 6: Make high-risk actions human-gated

One of the most useful patterns for enterprise agents is separating recommendation from execution.

For example:

Telemetry
    ↓
AI Agent
    ↓
Diagnosis
    ↓
Recommended Action
    ↓
Risk Check
    ↓
Human Approval
    ↓
Production Change

The agent might recommend:

	“Increase the database connection pool.”

But it shouldn’t push that change to production just because the model generated the recommendation.

Here’s what a simple approval boundary looks like:

Python
def execute_action(
    action: str,
    approved_by: str | None,
) -> dict:
    if not approved_by:
        return {
            "status": "awaiting_approval",
            "action": action,
        }

    return {
        "status": "approved",
        "action": action,
        "approved_by": approved_by,
    }

A real system needs a more sophisticated implementation, but the architectural boundary is what matters.

“The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation.”

The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation.

Step 7: Give the agent a health check

A production agent needs a health endpoint just like any other service.

With FastAPI:

`Python
import os

import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response, status

app = FastAPI()

SERVICE_NAME = "incident-command-agent"


@app.get("/health/live")
async def liveness():
    """Check whether the application process is responsive."""
    return {
        "status": "alive",
        "service": SERVICE_NAME,
    }


async def check_provider() -> bool:
    """Check a configured provider health endpoint."""
    health_url = os.getenv("MODEL_PROVIDER_HEALTH_URL")

    if not health_url:
        return False

    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=2.0) as client:
            result = await client.get(health_url)
            return result.status_code == 200
    except httpx.RequestError:
        return False


@app.get("/health/ready")
async def readiness(response: Response):
    """Check whether required dependencies are available."""
    if not await check_provider():
        response.status_code = (
            status.HTTP_503_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
        )
        return {
            "status": "unhealthy",
            "reason": "Model provider unavailable",
        }

    return {
        "status": "ready",
        "service": SERVICE_NAME,
    }

Liveness and readiness serve different purposes. The liveness endpoint confirms that the application process is responsive, while readiness checks whether the service can handle requests based on the availability of its required dependencies.

In this example, the readiness endpoint checks a configured model-provider health URL and returns HTTP 503 when the check fails. The check is deliberately lightweight and time-limited to avoid introducing unnecessary delays or costs. In production, teams should adapt it to their provider’s supported health-check mechanism and other critical dependencies, such as a vector database or configuration service.

Keeping these checks separate lets orchestration platforms such as Kubernetes distinguish between an application that needs restarting and one that can’t serve traffic temporarily.

Step 8: Fail closed when safety controls break

One of the worst failure modes is letting an agent keep running after its safety mechanisms go down.

For example:

Python
def run_controlled_agent(
    tool_name: str,
    model,
    messages,
    budget: ExecutionBudget,
):
    try:
        authorize_tool(tool_name)

        # Reuse the budget across agent steps and tool calls.
        budget.check_step()
        budget.check_tool_call()

        return invoke_model(
            model,
            messages,
        )

    except ToolAuthorizationError:
        logger.exception(
            "Agent authorisation check failed."
        )

        return {
            "status": "blocked",
            "message": (
                "The requested operation is not authorised."
            ),
        }

    except RuntimeError:
        logger.exception(
            "Agent execution budget exceeded."
        )

        return {
            "status": "escalated",
            "message": (
                "The agent exceeded its execution budget. "
                "Human investigation is required."
            ),
        }

    except Exception as exc:
        return handle_agent_failure(exc)

Notice that different failures produce different outcomes. An authorisation failure should block the requested operation, while an exhausted execution budget should trigger escalation rather than another retry. A temporary model failure, meanwhile, should follow the system’s defined failure-handling policy.

Another important detail: the execution budget must persist throughout the agent’s workflow. Creating a new budget for every invocation would reset its counters, allowing repeated calls to bypass the intended limits. Instead, create the budget once and pass it into each successive invocation, as shown below.

Python
# Create one budget for the entire agent workflow.
budget = ExecutionBudget(
    max_steps=5,
    max_tools=8,
)

# Reuse the same budget across successive invocations.
for tool_name in planned_tools:
    result = run_controlled_agent(
        tool_name=tool_name,
        model=model,
        messages=messages,
        budget=budget,
    )

    if isinstance(result, dict) and result.get(
        "status"
    ) in {"blocked", "escalated"}:
        break

With the same budget shared across invocations, each counted step and tool call contributes to the workflow’s overall limit. Once that limit is reached, the agent stops rather than continuing with a fresh budget. These controls only work if they remain effective throughout execution, especially when an agent encounters repeated failures.

Step 9: Define the 2 a.m. runbook

This is where operational ownership becomes real.

Suppose the agent starts failing at 2 a.m.

The on-call engineer should be able to answer five questions quickly:

  1. Is the agent itself healthy?
  2. Is the model provider healthy?
  3. Are retrieval or tool dependencies failing?
  4. Has the agent exceeded its normal cost or latency envelope?
  5. What happens if we disable it?

The last question matters most.

Every production AI system should have a clear degradation path.

For an incident-response agent, that might mean:

AI Agent unavailable
        ↓
Incident still created
        ↓
Telemetry remains available
        ↓
Standard runbook activated
        ↓
Human engineer continues investigation

The AI system should speed up operations, not become something the organisation can’t operate without.

So, who owns the agent?

The answer should never simply be:

	“The AI Team.”

Production ownership needs to be explicit.

Someone owns:

  • deployment;
  • infrastructure;
  • model configuration;
  • tool permissions;
  • monitoring;
  • incident response;
  • cost;
  • security;
  • rollback;
  • the decision to disable the agent.

That doesn’t mean one person has to handle everything. It means everyone knows their role well enough that, when an incident hits, the team isn’t wasting time figuring out who should take charge.

The real test of an AI agent

The easiest time to operate an AI agent is during business hours when everything is working. 

The real test comes at 2 a.m. 

A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget that prevents runaway behaviour, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries that constrain what it can do, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it.

The goal isn’t to take humans out of the loop.

“A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it.”

It’s to make it clear where the agent’s responsibility ends and where a human needs to step in.

Because when something goes wrong at 2 a.m., the question isn’t whether the model was smart enough.

It’s whether the system was designed well enough that the person on call knows what happened, what the agent did, and what to do next.

The post Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership appeared first on The New Stack.
When an AI agent breaks at 2 a.m., who gets paged? Discover how to build production ownership, guardrails, and runbooks for AI agents.

item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
One of the biggest security scares to hit the web is causing widespread disruption, prompting businesses, hospitals, schools, and government

The post PHP’s security scramble is just a preview: AI is digging up flaws faster than maintainers can fix them appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest security scares to hit the web is causing widespread disruption, prompting businesses, hospitals, schools, and government agencies to temporarily shut down websites and online services as they scramble to protect themselves against two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language underpinning much of the internet.

The vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code on affected servers. Major technology companies have been racing to protect users, with Cloudflare deploying firewall protections and Automattic confirming that websites hosted across its platforms, including WordPress.com, WordPress VIP and Tumblr, have been secured. The Wikimedia Foundation, meanwhile, took several supporting services offline until they can be patched.

The PHP project released emergency fixes on Wednesday for versions 8.2 through 8.5. Older versions are no longer officially supported, although some distributions and vendors provide legacy fixes, and PHP has published limited patches for versions 7.4 through 8.1.

But while the PHP vulnerabilities are a major deal in their own right, the circumstances surrounding their discovery, remediation, and disclosure offer a revealing glimpse into the growing pressures facing the open-source community, as AI makes it easier to uncover serious security flaws.

“Find bad vulnerabilities in PHP”: Prompt discovery

News of the impending patches emerged on Tuesday, after details leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. The following day, OpenAI revealed that security firm Calif had discovered one of the flaws using its GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google-owned Wiz had independently identified both vulnerabilities. OpenAI said it spent two months coordinating a response involving PHP maintainers, the security researchers, Cloudflare, and government cybersecurity agencies, as part of its Patch the Planet initiative.

The effort was disrupted when software supply-chain security company Chainguard released patched PHP container images more than six hours before the agreed time. CEO Dan Lorenc acknowledged on LinkedIn that he made the call, noting that Chainguard had independently rediscovered the flaw using a frontier AI model and the simple prompt “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP“.

Lorenc defended the decision by pointing to reports of attacks and the ease of reproducing the vulnerability. The PHP Foundation, for its part, argued that the early release could help attackers while other vendors were still preparing their patches.

“This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure,” the Foundation notes.

Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member and creator and co-maintainer of Composer, says that “there were no confirmed exploits,” adding that any identified activity was merely people attempting exploits.

“The decision you took unilaterally without any communication with the PHP team was both irresponsible and unprofessional.”

“There was a clear embargo until the time of disclosure and public release, that was discussed and evaluated repeatedly as information arrived, weighing the risk of exploitation vs protection from publishing patches without complete updates,” Adermann writes in response to Lorenc’s post. “The decision you took unilaterally without any communication with the PHP team was both irresponsible and unprofessional. The proper thing to do here is apologize, not to justify your clear misbehavior.”

The new normal

The PHP pandemonium highlights a larger concern, however: AI is making it easier to find security flaws, faster than the people responsible for fixing them can respond. And as Lorenc himself put it: “This is unfortunately the new normal for the industry.”

Just a day before OpenAI’s disclosure, Anthropic published research showing that Claude had identified 493 security issues across 25 open-source projects encompassing more than five million lines of code. One configuration flaw had gone unnoticed for 21 years, and had the potential to disable an authentication requirement, allowing unauthorised clients to reach a supposedly restricted server.

While not all of Anthropic’s findings were exploitable vulnerabilities, they underline a growing problem: AI can uncover security weaknesses at scale, but assessing them and developing reliable fixes still takes time and expertise.

Christopher Robinson, CTO of Akrites and CTO / chief security architect at the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), says the PHP emergency is also a reminder of the importance of being ready to respond when serious vulnerabilities do emerge.

“The best way to minimize the impact of events like PHP2Shell is to prepare and plan for these things to happen.”

“The best way to minimize the impact of events like PHP2Shell is to prepare and plan for these things to happen,” Robinson tells The New Stack. “Having a vulnerability management process and understanding who can assist when issues become too complex are the best things that both open source projects and commercial entities can do.”

When finding bugs becomes easier than fixing them

For Michelle Tilley, software engineer and CTO of Atuin, an open-source developer tool with more than 32,000 GitHub stars, the kind of emergency response mounted for PHP would be difficult to replicate for smaller open-source projects.

“The response here looked like a vendor emergency, with a coalition, government agencies, and WAF (web application firewall) rules,” Tilley tells The New Stack. “This works for a project like PHP, but no one is going to assemble a coalition for an obscure 3-maintainer library that turns out to be used in software all around the world.”

“This works for a project like PHP, but no one is going to assemble a coalition for an obscure 3-maintainer library that turns out to be used in software all around the world.”

Atuin itself is already receiving more AI-generated bug reports and pull requests, Tilley says. While her company has enough engineering resources to handle them, many smaller projects depend on unpaid maintainers working in their spare time, who can become overwhelmed and walk away.

“These developers can, and do, burn out,” Tilley continues. “Sometimes they arrange for someone else to take over the project; often, they simply stop working on it, and downstream consumers never know. That’s how projects end up with vulnerabilities that will never be patched.”

Ultimately, she wants more responsibility to fall on researchers and businesses that rely on the code.

“There’s no single fix, but the direction is clear,” Tilley says. “The cost of remediation has to move toward the people finding the bugs and the companies depending on the code.”

That pressure extends to larger projects, too. Madelyn Olson, an AWS principal engineer and maintainer of the Valkey database, says that it too is finding and fixing far more security bugs this year than before.

“The hardest part has shifted from finding bugs to fixing them,” Olson tells The New Stack. “PHP is a good example.”

A PHP developer first identified the underlying problem behind one of this week’s vulnerabilities while fixing an issue uncovered during a 2024 security audit, which was organised by the Open Source Technology Improvement Fund (OSTIF). However, attempts to resolve it stalled because proposed fixes risked breaking compatibility, affecting performance or disrupting third-party extensions. Few engineers had the expertise to resolve those trade-offs, according to the PHP Foundation.

“AI is getting very good at finding bugs,” Olson says. “Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.”

“AI is getting very good at finding bugs. Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.”

To manage the influx, Valkey is narrowing its definition of a security vulnerability, using AI to inspect its own code, and making backports and releases easier to produce.

The Chainguard brouhaha also raises the question of whether disclosure timelines need to change. Olson recalls three researchers independently reporting the same Valkey bug in one week, each using LLMs. Valkey is now working toward shorter embargoes — although that is a different matter from breaking an agreed release date.

“If you found a bug with an LLM, it’s safe to say someone else can find it too,” Olson says. “That argues for shorter embargoes and faster releases, and Valkey is working toward shorter embargoes now, which is a trend we’re seeing across most large projects.”

A growing security backlog

Derek Zimmer, executive director of OSTIF, said the volume of both legitimate discoveries and poor-quality reports is creating backlogs, with maintainers spending scarce engineering time just establishing which issues are real.

“Maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage.”

“The reality in 2026 is that finding serious bugs is easier than ever, and maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage,” Zimmer tells The New Stack.

To help, OSTIF is trialling initiatives such as Project V-LAT, which embeds engineers in projects to review findings and develop fixes, while helping maintainers improve how reports are processed.

Robinson also emphasises the need for shared security expertise and dedicated engineers who can support upstream projects. He rejects the suggestion that exposing more flaws necessarily makes open source less secure, pointing to the opportunity for companies that depend on the code to contribute fixes. Yet, many projects have neither the money nor the expertise to respond independently.

“Most upstream maintainers are also acting as volunteers within the projects, with little to no budget, infrastructure, or supporting tools,” Robinson says. “There will be no ‘one size fits all’ approach here, we’ll need to approach this situation using multiple, parallel approaches to get the broadest chance for successful outcomes.”

The post PHP’s security scramble is just a preview: AI is digging up flaws faster than maintainers can fix them appeared first on The New Stack.
PHP2Shell’s chaotic disclosure sparked a row. Behind the drama, maintainers warn that AI is piling new security work onto already stretched teams.

item.title: DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 vs. Claude Haiku 5.5: More accurate at a fraction of the price
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017 on October 17 as an update to its Flash model. Its change log says the update cuts

The post DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 vs. Claude Haiku 5.5: More accurate at a fraction of the price appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017 on October 17 as an update to its Flash model. Its change log says the update cuts task runtime and output length. It lists 11 benchmark scores, including 42.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0.

Developers can use it through DeepSeek’s API or a service like OpenRouter. Because it’s an open-weight model, they can also download it from Hugging Face and run it on their own servers. I tested it through OpenRouter on DeepSeek’s own servers, at DeepSeek’s prices.

DeepSeek’s model card compares the update with several rivals, but not Haiku 5.5, so I picked it for this hands-on comparison. Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7 as its fastest model at standard speed, aimed at high-volume tasks such as classification, summarization, and database queries.

Anthropic notes that its Opus models run faster in Fast Mode. Anthropic reports 39.2 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 3.1 percentage points below DeepSeek’s reported score. These are vendor-reported results, rather than a controlled head-to-head test.

Haiku costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, then $0.50 and $2.50 above that. DeepSeek’s off-peak rates are $0.15 per million uncached input tokens, $0.003 per million cached input tokens, and $0.60 per million output tokens; peak rates are twice those amounts.

Comparing uncached input and output rates, Haiku is cheaper on short prompts, and DeepSeek is cheaper on long ones. Actual charges also depend on tokenization, caching, and the provider route.

I built three tests around what each company says its model does well to see which one performs better in practice.

The tests

I ran both models once per test through OpenRouter, pinned to DeepSeek’s and Anthropic’s own servers, at default settings. I pinned DeepSeek to model ID 1017 and ran everything off-peak. A script graded every answer against keys I built and checked with a second method before either model saw them.

  • Agentic bug fix: A Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one wrong test. The model reads, edits, and runs tests through tools, with a 25-turn cap.
  • Database queries: A fake CI platform database with 20 questions, answered by writing SQL. Traps include soft deletes, mixed casing, retried builds, time zones, and currency conversion. Two questions can’t be answered from the data.
  • Triage: 400 developer error reports, each needing a category, a severity, a service, and a team. That’s 1,600 scored fields. The prompt counted as 153,082 input tokens on DeepSeek and 216,811 on Haiku, past Haiku’s 100,000-token price threshold.

Agentic bug fix

DeepSeek started strong, beating Haiku’s accuracy on the first test. DeepSeek scored 6 of 6. Haiku scored 5 of 6. Both found the first bug even though the error pointed at the wrong file, fixed the third, broke no regression tests, and flagged the wrong test without touching it. Haiku missed one of six hidden tests on the second bug, and DeepSeek didn’t.

Haiku finished in eight turns and 21.6 seconds. DeepSeek took 12 turns and 49.6 seconds but still cost less because it automatically cached most of the repeated input. I didn’t turn on Anthropic’s prompt caching, which requires an opt-in. This compares the caching settings used in these runs; enabling Haiku’s caching could change the cost comparison.

The numbers:

  • DeepSeek: 12 calls, 190,139 in, 7,877 out, $0.009, 49.6 s.
  • Haiku: 8 calls, 100,461 in, 3,255 out, $0.012, 21.6 s.

Database queries

This is the only test where both models tied for accuracy, both scoring 20 out of 20. Both caught every trap and answered “unknown” to both questions the data couldn’t answer rather than hallucinating. Haiku got the answers in fewer calls and less time. DeepSeek cost about half as much.

The numbers:

  • DeepSeek: 12 calls, 75,151 in, 4,608 out, $0.004, 34.9 s.
  • Haiku 7 calls, 55,304 in, 5,917 out, $0.009, 28.4 s.

Triage

Here’s where the accuracy differences are clearest. DeepSeek got all 1,600 fields right. Haiku got 1,596. Two of its misses were severity ratings. The routing guide rates a report sev4 if it affects fewer than 50 users or has an error rate under 1%. Haiku rated a report with 49 affected customers as sev3, and another with a 0.8% error rate as sev3. Both should have been sev4. 

Haiku’s other two misses were routing mistakes. The guide says one service moved to a new team on August 1 and that reports should be routed by the date in their header. Haiku sent two reports filed after August 1 to the old team. Each mentioned an earlier July date in its body, but the outputs alone don’t explain why Haiku chose the old team.
